questions.question:
Answer the examiner's questions about yourself.

What's your name? Where do you live?
Do you work or are you a student?
What do you enjoy most about your studies or your job? Why?
How do you usually travel to your school, college or workplace?
Tell us about a teacher or a colleague who has helped you.
What would you like to study or do in the future?
questions.explanation: Give full answers, not just one or two words: add a reason or an example (e.g. 'I enjoy biology most because I like learning how the body works'). Use present simple for routines, past simple for the story about a teacher or colleague, and would like / going to / hope to for the future. Grammar and vocabulary, pronunciation and interactive communication are assessed.

questions.question:
Look at the photograph. It shows a group of four young people working together at a large table in a bright office. One woman is pointing at a laptop screen, a man is writing notes on a whiteboard, and two others are looking at papers and smiling. There are coffee cups and coloured sticky notes on the table.

Tell us what you can see in the photograph. Talk for about one minute.
questions.explanation: Describe the people, what they are doing, where they are and what things you can see, using the present continuous ('A woman is pointing at...', 'They're discussing...'). Use there is / there are, prepositions of place (on the left, in the background, next to) and guesses with might / may / looks like ('They might be planning a project'). If you don't know a word, explain it in other words ('small pieces of paper you can stick on things'). Keep talking for about a minute.

questions.question:
A group of students from your school has some free time on Saturday mornings and wants to do a short course together. Here are some courses they could choose:

a cooking course
a first aid course
a computer programming course
a photography course
a course in a foreign language
a course on how to start a small business

Talk together about the different courses the students could do, and say which would be the most useful for them. Then decide which course they should choose. Talk for about two or three minutes.
questions.explanation: Discuss several of the options with your partner before deciding; do not just describe them one by one. Give opinions with reasons ('A first aid course would be useful because you never know when someone might need help'), ask your partner's view ('What do you think?', 'Do you agree?'), agree and disagree politely ('That's a good point, but...') and reach a decision together at the end ('So shall we choose...?'). Interactive communication is especially important in this part.

questions.question:
Answer the examiner's questions and discuss them with your partner.

Do you prefer studying on your own or with other people? Why?
Is it a good idea for students to have a part-time job? Why or why not?
What skills do you think are most important for finding a good job today?
Would you like to work in an office, or somewhere else? Why?
Tell us about something new you have learnt recently. How did you learn it?
Do you think people will study more online in the future?
questions.explanation: Give your opinion and support it with reasons and examples from your own experience. Respond to what your partner says ('I agree with you, because...', 'I see what you mean, but...') and ask their opinion. Use present perfect for recent experiences ('I've just learnt to...'), comparatives for preferences ('It's easier to concentrate on my own') and will / might for the future.
